title: Managing Project Execution
sequence: Executing follows Planning and runs alongside Monitoring & Controlling until Closing. Predictive projects execute against baselines; adaptive projects execute in iterations, each with its own planning, execution and review.

header.html: Executing is the setting in which several ECO tasks are carried out rather than a task of its own. It supports Process Task 1 (the execution strategy in practice; data to make informed decisions), Process Task 9 (create, update, document and keep artifacts accessible; work performance data), Business Environment Tasks 3 and 4 (implement approved changes; remove impediments), and People Tasks 3, 7 and 8 (lead the team, transfer knowledge, communicate).

Topic 14 (plan, execution strategy, data to decisions) · Topic 18 (Manage Quality Assurance) · Topic 19 (Acquire Resources) · Topic 20 (Manage Communications) · Topic 21 (Implement Risk Responses) · Topic 25 (Lead the Team) · Topic 26 (conflict) · Topic 27 (Manage Project Knowledge) · Topic 28 (status and metrics) · Topic 29 (change control) · Topic 30 (issues and impediments)

Standard §4.5.3 Executing Focus Area · Guide §2.1.6.4 Manage Project Execution (Governance domain) · Section 4 artifacts (deliverables, work performance data, issue log, change requests, approved change requests, change log, lessons learned register) · Section 5 tools (PMIS, meetings, daily coordination meetings, colocation, virtual teams)

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Term Meaning
Executing Focus Area The processes, practices or actions performed to complete the work consistently with the currently agreed course of action: coordinating resources, managing stakeholder engagement, performing project activities and other project tasks
Key benefit Focused execution that delivers the value proposition in the integrated baseline; the project management plan can and should change whenever the change would enhance the value proposition; the choice of development approach (adaptive, predictive or hybrid) is most visible here
Manage Project Execution Leading and performing the work defined in the plan and implementing approved changes to meet project objectives; allocating resources and managing their use; adjusting plans from analysis of work performance data
Deliverable Any unique, verifiable product, result or capability produced to complete a process, phase or project
Work performance data Raw observations and measurements from the work (work completed, KPIs, technical performance measures, actual start and finish dates, story points completed, deliverable status, schedule progress, number of change requests and defects, actual costs and durations)
Change request A formal proposal to modify a document, deliverable or baseline; may be internal or external; types include corrective action, preventive action, defect repair and updates
Approved change request A change processed under the change management plan and approved, deferred or rejected; approved ones are implemented through Manage Project Execution; deferred and rejected ones are communicated to the requester
Change log List of submitted changes with status and disposition
Issue log Document where issues are recorded and monitored
PMIS The project management information system: scheduling tools, work authorization systems, configuration management, information collection and distribution, automated KPI reporting
Daily coordination meeting A brief team meeting (no more than 15 minutes) on yesterday's progress, today's plan and obstacles; key to self-direction in agile work

2What Runs in the Executing Focus Area

Process Domain Covered in
Manage Project Execution Governance This topic
Manage Quality Assurance Governance Topic 18
Manage Project Knowledge Governance Topic 27
Manage Stakeholder Engagement Stakeholders Topic 13
Manage Communications Stakeholders Topic 20
Acquire Resources Resources Topic 19
Lead the Team Resources Topics 25 and 26
Implement Risk Responses Risk Topic 21

Scope, Schedule and Finance have no Executing-only process: their work is planned in Planning and controlled in Monitoring & Controlling, while the work they describe is performed here. Monitoring and Controlling runs in parallel and receives the work performance data.

3Manage Project Execution

Purpose: align the knowledge and skills of all team members toward the objectives ("the collective team has more knowledge than any single person"); produce deliverables from activities carried out according to the plan; make the whole of technical and functional work fit together in the wider project ecosystem.

Aspect Detail
Inputs Any component of the project management plan; change log, lessons learned register, milestone list, project communications, schedule, requirements traceability matrix, risk register and report; approved change requests; EEFs and OPAs
Tools Expert judgment, PMIS, meetings (including daily coordination meetings)
Outputs Deliverables, work performance data, issue log, change requests, project management plan and document updates (activity list, assumption log, lessons learned, requirements documentation, risk and stakeholder registers), OPA updates
Also includes Reviewing the impact of all changes and implementing approved ones: corrective actions, preventive actions and defect remediation
Quality in execution Two routes: process quality assurance (Manage Quality Assurance) and deliverable quality through scope management and control; deliverables must be produced to the agreed requirements in the scope baseline (in adaptive work: prioritized requirements or the sprint backlog)

4Directing and Managing the Work Day to Day

Activity What good looks like
Start well A kickoff aligned on vision, plan, roles and team agreements (the team charter, Topic 19); a shared understanding of how work is authorized and reported
Assign and coordinate Work assigned per the plan and responsibility assignment matrix; handoffs and confirmation points defined; dependencies and interfaces managed; contractor work coordinated with clear reporting lines between vendor supervisors and the team (Topic 22)
Keep the plan alive When reality or value changes, use the change process (predictive) or reprioritize the backlog (adaptive); the plan is not an unchangeable contract
Collect work performance data Capture actual dates, costs, effort, progress, defects and story points consistently so Monitoring & Controlling can turn data into information (Topic 14, section 11)
Keep information accessible Use the PMIS; keep approved artifacts in a controlled repository; apply configuration control so people use current versions; make progress visible to stakeholders
Remove impediments Evaluate, prioritize and remove blockers; reassess whether a resolved blocker has really ended or has shifted (Topic 30)
Engage stakeholders and communicate Run the engagement and communications plans (Topics 13 and 20); meetings with agendas and recorded actions
Implement risk responses and quality assurance Risk owners execute responses; audits and reviews run on schedule (Topics 18 and 21)
Develop and lead the team Coach, recognize, resolve conflict early (Topics 25 and 26)
Capture knowledge as you go Lessons learned during the work, not only at the end (Topic 27)
Protect value Watch the business case and external changes; do not let output replace outcomes (Topics 10 and 33)

5Implementing Approved Changes

  1. Any stakeholder may request a change; requests are assessed through Assess and Implement Changes (Topic 29) with impact on all domains.
  2. The change is approved, deferred or rejected; the disposition goes in the change log and is communicated (including to those whose requests were deferred or rejected).
  3. Manage Project Execution implements approved changes (corrective actions, preventive actions, defect repairs, updates).
  4. Update everything affected: drawings or designs, schedule and baselines, backlog, requirements documents, risk register; an approval is not complete until the work and the documents reflect it.
  5. Do not make unapproved changes, even harmless-looking or free ones (a free design improvement, a higher-capacity part): evaluate the impact and submit them through change control; checking that tests pass does not replace configuration review.

6Executing in Adaptive and Hybrid Work

  • Iterations are small execution cycles: plan the iteration from the backlog and actual team capacity; work within the definition of done; hold the daily coordination meeting; review the increment with stakeholders (with feedback time); hold a retrospective and commit to a few improvements (Topic 04).
  • Plan on real capacity. If members are partly assigned elsewhere, the sprint scope shrinks accordingly; do not keep the scope and ask the team to "be more efficient".
  • Protect the iteration: mid-iteration requests from executives go to the product owner and the backlog; the project manager represents the team's capacity and shows the trade-off.
  • Quality is built in: automated tests and compliance checks are part of the definition of done, not a late testing phase (Topic 18).
  • Make progress visible: information radiators, burn charts and boards in a place stakeholders can see; a burnup shows whether slow progress is really growing scope.
  • Remove impediments proactively; raising the same blocker in every stand-up without action is not management.
  • Hybrid: executives see milestones with iterations beneath; fixed regulatory or contractual commitments are executed under change control, while the iterative layer adapts within those boundaries.

7Event Routing: What to Do When Things Happen

Rules of thumb:

  • Check the plan and agreements first, then act within them; escalate only what is outside your scope or authority.
  • A risk that occurs is an issue; a recurring impediment needs action, not another log entry.
  • Never skip the record: change log, issue log, risk register, lessons learned register and the backlog are how decisions survive turnover and audits.
  • When two teams or parties miss handoffs, define the handoff, responsibilities and confirmation points instead of adding meetings.

8Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Unit of execution Work packages and activities against the baselines, phase by phase Iterations from a prioritized backlog Baselined envelope with iterations inside
Authorizing work Per the plan and work authorization Team pulls work from the sprint backlog; product owner prioritizes Both
Coordination Status meetings, dependency management, PMO Daily coordination, shared boards, reviews Both
Change Formal change requests, CCB, baseline updates Backlog reprioritization, product owner, retrospectives; formal approval only above contract thresholds Change control for the envelope only
Data Actuals vs baseline; EV Velocity, burn charts, cycle time, accepted work Both
Quality Inspections, reviews, tests at defined points DoD in every iteration; continuous testing Both
Leadership Direction and coordination Servant leadership, self-organization, impediment removal Mix

9Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

  • Tailor execution rhythm, formality of work authorization, meeting cadence and documentation to project size, risk, regulation, team distribution and culture.
  • Interactions: execution turns the plans of every domain into work: scope (deliverables), schedule (activities and iterations), finance (spending), resources (team and physical resources), stakeholders (engagement), risk (responses) and governance (decisions and escalation).
  • How to tell execution is healthy: deliverables are produced to requirements and verified; work performance data are collected regularly; issues and impediments are cleared; changes follow the process and documents stay current; stakeholders are engaged and informed; lessons are captured as the work goes.

10Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Approved changes must be implemented and the documents updated (drawings, schedule, backlog); approval alone does not finish the change.
  2. Unapproved changes, even free or beneficial ones, go through change control. Do not just remove or keep them without review.
  3. Follow the plan, but change it when value demands it: through the change process, not informally.
  4. Mid-iteration requests go through the backlog and the product owner; protect the team's capacity.
  5. Plan the iteration on actual capacity. Do not keep scope and demand more efficiency.
  6. Remove impediments; recurring ones need action, and resolved ones need follow-up to confirm they have not shifted.
  7. Define handoffs, roles and reporting lines (internal and vendor) rather than adding review meetings.
  8. Collect work performance data consistently so that status is based on facts.
  9. Make progress transparent where stakeholders can see it.
  10. A risk that occurs is an issue: execute the planned response.
  11. Build quality in during execution; do not rely on a final phase to find defects.
  12. Capture lessons while working; do not wait for closure.
  13. Resolve conflict early and at the source; do not let it grow.
  14. Check the agreed plan, documents and contracts first, then act within them.
  15. Do not confuse execution with control: execution produces deliverables and data; control analyzes and decides on corrective action.
  16. Execution is not "heads-down": it includes engaging stakeholders, communicating, coordinating resources and leading the team.

11Exam Q&A

11.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1During the month, the team completes planned activities and records the actual dates, costs, defects and story points. Which process produces these outputs?

  • AManage Quality Assurance, which audits the data for conformance with processes
  • BManage Project Execution, which yields deliverables and work performance data
  • CMonitor and Control Scope, which analyzes the data and decides on corrective action
  • DDevelop Schedule, which converts the data into an approved schedule baseline
Show the answer

Answer: B. Executing produces deliverables and the raw work performance data (actual dates, costs, defects, points), while monitoring and controlling turns the data into information and decides on action. Developing the schedule and auditing processes are different activities.

S2To avoid a probable slip in the next sprint, the team proposes adding a second tester before the slip occurs. Which type of change request is this?

  • APreventive action, which reduces the probability of a future negative result
  • BCorrective action, which brings current performance back in line with the plan
  • CDefect repair, which brings a nonconforming component into compliance
  • DBaseline update, which records approved scope in the project documents
Show the answer

Answer: A. A preventive action reduces the probability of future negative consequences, whereas a corrective action realigns current performance with the plan and a defect repair fixes a nonconforming component. A baseline update records an approved change and is not the request type here.

S3An inspection finds that three delivered panels do not meet the specification, and the team raises a request to fix them. Which type of change request is this?

  • AScope change, which adds new features to the design of the panels
  • BCorrective action, which realigns the schedule with the baseline
  • CPreventive action, which reduces the chance of a future defect occurring
  • DDefect repair, which brings the nonconforming panels into compliance
Show the answer

Answer: D. Defect repair modifies a defective or nonconforming component to bring it into compliance. Preventive and corrective actions address future probability or performance against the plan, and a scope change alters what is to be delivered.

S4A hybrid project starts with each member receiving an email of tasks, and by week two people disagree about who decides what. What would have prevented the confusion?

  • ATask assignments in more detail, with a daily written report from each member
  • BA kickoff aligned on vision, roles, team agreements and how work is authorized
  • CA status meeting reviewing the percentage of tasks completed so far
  • DA formal review of the schedule baseline by the steering committee
Show the answer

Answer: B. A good start aligns the team on vision, plan, roles, team agreements and how work is authorized and reported, which settles decision rights early. More task detail, status reviews or a baseline review do not create shared agreements.

S5Three scrum teams report progress in hours, story points and tasks finished respectively, and the project manager cannot consolidate the status. What should the project manager do?

  • AAsk the leads to send narrative updates and rely on the overall impression
  • BConvert each lead's figures using the project manager's own estimates of progress
  • CChoose the lead whose method looks best and ignore the other two sets of figures
  • DAgree one set of measures and progress rules, and collect data consistently
Show the answer

Answer: D. Status rests on work performance data collected consistently, with agreed units and rules of performance measurement, so that monitoring can turn data into information. Converting by guesswork, narratives or ignoring two leads gives unreliable or incomplete status.

S6Halfway through an iteration, the team can see that it will not finish all committed stories. What should the project manager do?

  • AAsk the team to work overtime until every committed story is completed
  • BHelp the team and product owner agree which stories to swap or drop to protect the goal
  • CExtend the iteration by a week so that all of the stories can be finished
  • DWait for the iteration review and report the unfinished stories there
Show the answer

Answer: B. The commitment is protected by acting early: the team and the product owner renegotiate scope, swapping or dropping the lowest-value stories to keep the iteration goal. Overtime, stretching the timebox or waiting for the review hides the problem or breaks the fixed iteration.

S7A new project manager believes execution means keeping the team heads-down in its sprints and says stakeholders can be updated when deliverables are ready. Two stakeholders are now surprised by a design change. What was misunderstood?

  • AExecution also includes engaging stakeholders and communicating with them
  • BExecution means analyzing variances and deciding on corrective actions
  • CExecution is the team's job, and the project manager only observes it
  • DExecution begins only after every single stakeholder has signed off every plan
Show the answer

Answer: A. Executing includes engaging stakeholders, communicating, coordinating resources and leading the team, as well as producing deliverables. Analyzing variances is control, execution does not wait for universal sign-off, and the project manager actively leads it.

S8Early user feedback shows that a module in the baselined plan will no longer bring value, and the team asks whether it must still be built. What should the project manager do?

  • ADrop the module quietly and use the saved time on other planned work
  • BBuild it as planned, since the baseline is a commitment that cannot be altered
  • CUse the change process to remove or replace it, since value justifies change
  • DBuild a smaller version of the module to hedge, without any approval
Show the answer

Answer: C. The plan can and should change whenever the change enhances the value proposition, through the change process rather than informally. Building to the baseline regardless, dropping work quietly or hedging without approval ignores value or governance.

S9The approved response to a vendor-delay risk has a named owner, and the trigger has occurred, yet the owner says other work comes first and nothing has been done. What should the project manager do?

  • ACarry out the response personally without informing the owner or the sponsor
  • BRemove the owner's name from the register and mark the risk as accepted
  • CSupport the owner to carry out the response, and escalate if needed
  • DWait for the vendor delay to occur and log it as an issue at that point
Show the answer

Answer: C. Risk owners carry out the agreed responses, with the project manager influencing and supporting, and escalating if the owner cannot act. Acting without informing anyone, waiting for the delay or relabeling the risk as accepted abandons the planned response.

S10Mechanical and electrical subcontractors each finished their work packages on time, but the panels do not fit the ducts. Which execution activity was missed?

  • AManaging dependencies and interfaces by defining the fit points with both teams
  • BResource leveling of the two subcontractors' crews across the schedule
  • CQuality audits of each subcontractor's internal documentation and procedures
  • DWeekly status reports from each subcontractor on its percentage complete
Show the answer

Answer: A. Executing includes coordinating dependencies and interfaces among teams so the pieces fit together in the wider ecosystem; each package passed its own checks but no one owned the interface. Audits, leveling or percentage-complete reports do not control where the pieces meet.

11.2 Recall Q&As

R1What does the Executing Focus Area do?

Show the answer

Completes the work consistently with the currently agreed course of action: coordinating resources, managing stakeholder engagement and performing activities; the plan can change whenever a change enhances value.

R2What is Manage Project Execution?

Show the answer

Leading and performing the work in the plan and implementing approved changes, allocating resources, and adjusting plans from analysis of work performance data.

R3What are the main outputs of Manage Project Execution?

Show the answer

Deliverables, work performance data, issue log, change requests, plan and document updates, OPA updates.

R4Which processes run in Executing besides Manage Project Execution?

Show the answer

Manage Quality Assurance, Manage Project Knowledge, Manage Stakeholder Engagement, Manage Communications, Acquire Resources, Lead the Team and Implement Risk Responses.

R5What types of change request exist?

Show the answer

Corrective action, preventive action, defect repair and updates.

R6What happens to deferred or rejected change requests?

Show the answer

They are recorded in the change log and communicated to the requester.

R7What is work performance data?

Show the answer

Raw observations and measurements such as work completed, actual dates and costs, story points done, defects and KPIs, passed to the controlling processes.

R8How is quality addressed in execution?

Show the answer

Through process quality assurance and through deliverable quality managed by scope management and control, against the scope baseline or sprint backlog.

R9What is a daily coordination meeting?

Show the answer

A brief (up to 15 minutes) team meeting on progress, today's plan and obstacles, supporting self-direction.

R10What is a PMIS?

Show the answer

An information system with tools for scheduling, work authorization, configuration management and information distribution, including automated KPI reporting.

R11What should be updated when a change is approved?

Show the answer

Plans, baselines, schedule, backlog, designs and other documents, and stakeholders must be informed.

R12Where do mid-iteration requests go?

Show the answer

To the product owner and the backlog, with capacity and trade-offs made visible.

R13What distinguishes execution from monitoring and control?

Show the answer

Execution performs the work and produces deliverables and data; monitoring and controlling compares, analyzes and recommends corrective action, in parallel.

R14What is the project manager's first move when a risk occurs?

Show the answer

Treat it as an issue: log it, execute the planned response, update the register and inform stakeholders.

12Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Executing Focus Area Complete work per the agreed course of action; plan can and should change when a change adds value
Manage Project Execution Lead and perform the work; implement approved changes; allocate resources; collect data
Outputs Deliverables, work performance data, issue log, change requests, updates
Other Executing processes Manage QA, Manage Project Knowledge, Manage Stakeholder Engagement, Manage Communications, Acquire Resources, Lead the Team, Implement Risk Responses
Change requests Corrective, preventive, defect repair, updates; approved, deferred or rejected
Approved change Implement; update plans, baselines, documents; communicate
Unapproved change Even free ones go through change control
Mid-iteration request Product owner and backlog; protect capacity
Capacity Plan on actual availability
Impediments Remove; reassess; escalate; do not just log
Handoffs and roles Define responsibilities, confirmation points and reporting lines (internal and vendor)
Transparency Progress visible where stakeholders can see it
Risk occurs It is an issue: execute response, update, inform
Quality Built in: DoD, early tests, QA audits
Data Collect work performance data consistently for monitoring and control
First-action pattern Check the plan and agreements, act within them, route events to the right owner and record, use change control, capture lessons, keep stakeholders informed
